Understanding the differences among experimental, non-experimental, and quasi-experimental designs can significantly impact the quality of research findings. Study design comparison illustrates the differences between various methodologies, including experimental, non-experimental, and quasi-experimental designs. Lastly, quasi-experimental designs share characteristics with experimental methods but lack random assignment, allowing researchers to study phenomena where full control isn’t feasible. Experimental designs are research methodologies aimed at establishing cause-and-effect relationships between variables. By contrasting experimental with non-experimental and quasi-experimental designs, one can appreciate the intricate dynamics involved in different research methodologies. Non-experimental designs play a crucial role in research as they allow for the observation and analysis of variables in their natural settings without manipulation. Unlike experimental designs, where researchers actively intervene or control variables, non-experimental designs observe variables as they naturally occur. One primary purpose of non-experimental designs is to provide descriptive data that can inform future research or policy decisions. Understanding non-experimental designs is essential for those involved in study design comparison, as they offer insights into real-world situations without imposing artificial constraints or biases. Study design comparison highlights the fundamental differences between experimental and non-experimental approaches. These designs are useful for exploratory research and can provide insights when experimentation is not feasible. In an experimental design, researchers actively manipulate independent variables to observe their effect on dependent variables. Understanding these differences is essential for effective study design comparison, guiding researchers in choosing the appropriate methodology based on their research goals and the required level of control over variables. In real-world research, the effectiveness of different study design comparisons can be observed in various contexts. Experimental designs often shine in clinical trials, allowing researchers to determine causality through random assignment and control groups. Quasi-experimental designs fill the gap between these two, using naturally occurring groups to assess effects, such as evaluating the educational outcomes of two different school curriculums. Researchers may opt for quasi-experimental designs when randomization is impractical or unethical, allowing for valuable insights into causal relationships without the rigid structure of traditional experiments. Quasi-experimental designs stand out in research due to their unique characteristics and features. When considering a study design comparison, it’s essential to recognize the strengths and weaknesses inherent in experimental, non-experimental, and quasi-experimental designs.

COMMON THREATS TO INTERNAL VALIDITY OF QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL DESIGNS EVALUATING INTERVENTIONS IN REAL-WORLD SETTINGS History bias: events other than the intervention occurring at the same time that may influence the results Selection bias: systematic differences in subject characteristics between the intervention and control groups that are related to the outcome Maturation bias: changes among individuals in the groups, differently over time, resulting in effects in addition to (or rather than) the treatment condition that may change the performance of participants in the posttest relative to the pretest Lack of blinding: awareness of group assignment that influences those delivering or receiving the intervention Differential dropout: attrition affecting the intervention or the control group differently, resulting in selection bias and/or loss of statistical power Variability in interactive effects: implementation of an intervention with multiple components that varies across the implementation process and/or by sites Source: Adapted from Reference 52 QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL DESIGNS FOR PROSPECTIVE EVALUTION OF INTERVENTIONS * QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL DESIGNS FOR PROSPECTIVE EVALUTION OF INTERVENTIONS * CONSIDERATIONS IN CHOOSING AMONG QEDs * STRATEGIES TO STRENGTHEN EXTERNAL VALIDITY Table 1 summarizes the main QEDs that have been used for prospective evaluation of health interventions in real-world settings: prepost designs with a nonequivalent control group, ITS, and SWDs. results.content: In stepped-wedge designs, the clusters are randomized into several groups or waves that define when the intervention will begin, and all clusters start the trial in the control condition. As of 2022, all of the NIH Pragmatic Trials Collaboratory Trials that used a stepped-wedge design were granted a waiver of consent (Federico et al 2022). Because of the staggered schedule of intervention rollout in the stepped-wedge design, this regulatory pause introduced a significant disruption to the trial’s implementation, and the researchers speculated that parallel randomization might have been better. Dr. Liz Turner discusses arguments for and against using the stepped-wedge design when choosing the right cluster randomized trial in pragmatic research. Title: Quasi-experimental methods | evaluation.treasury.gov.au
Quasi‑experimental methods are a broad group of research design and statistical methods that aim to identify the impact of a program or policy on outcomes of interest. Quasi‑experimental methods require us to make stronger assumptions that than RCT to confidently attribute a change in outcome to the program. For example, we might want to look at the impact of an academic scholarship on future income where receiving a scholarship is determined by being at or above a grade point average (GPA) of 6 in the third year of study. Because of this, a comparison of average post‑university income just around the GPA cut‑off can be used to estimate the causal impact of receiving a scholarship on future income. Difference‑in‑differences (DiD) is a widely used quasi‑experimental method that compares outcomes over time between those enrolled in a program and those who were not. This method requires data on the outcome over time in both groups, spanning the period before and after the program was delivered. First, we take the difference in average wellbeing scores between the start and end of the year within the division that received the gym membership. We need to calculate the difference in wellbeing scores between the start and end of the year among those that *didn’t receive the gym membership*. This difference should capture any factor that changes self‑reported wellbeing over time that isn’t related to the gym membership. This group stands in as our counterfactual, it tells us about the change in self‑reported wellbeing that we would expect to see if those that received the gym membership had not received it. By doing this we ‘clean’ our estimate of program impact of any influence of time varying factors. The main assumption that is required to interpret the DiD estimate as a causal effect of gym membership. We assume that distance from the pharmacy impacts blood pressure solely through the drug, and because of this any observed difference in blood pressure between those living further and closer from the pharmacy must be due to the impact of the drug. This gives us an accurate estimate of the drug’s impact **among those** who are influenced by the instrument (distance from the pharmacy) to take up the drug.

Electronic address: Christopher.Miller8@va.gov."), Shawna N Smith2, Marianne Pugatch3, United States Department of Veterans Affairs, Boston, MA, USA.") ### Affiliations * 1 VA Boston Healthcare System, Center for Healthcare Organization and Implementation Research (CHOIR), United States Department of Veterans Affairs, Boston, MA, USA; Department of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. 10.1016/j.psychres.2019.06.027 ## Abstract Implementation science is focused on maximizing the adoption, appropriate use, and sustainability of effective clinical practices in real world clinical settings. Many implementation science questions can be feasibly answered by fully experimental designs, typically in the form of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Other implementation science questions are more suited to quasi-experimental designs, which are intended to estimate the effect of an intervention in the absence of randomization. In this article we review the use of experimental designs in implementation science, including recent methodological advances for implementation studies. We also review the use of quasi-experimental designs in implementation science, and discuss the strengths and weaknesses of these approaches. This article is therefore meant to be a practical guide for researchers who are interested in selecting the most appropriate study design to answer relevant implementation science questions, and thereby increase the rate at which effective clinical practices are adopted, spread, and sustained.
